title: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
summary: How agents remember across sessions: episodic vs semantic memories, MemGPT's context hierarchy, Mem0's ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP write path, Generative Agents retrieval scoring, reflection, decay, evaluation, failure modes.
outcomes: Explain why replaying full history fails and what an agent should store as episodic versus semantic memory
Trace how MemGPT pages data between main context and external storage using self-editing function calls
Walk a new fact through extraction and the ADD, UPDATE, DELETE and NOOP update operations, resolving a conflict
Compute Generative Agents retrieval scores from recency decay, importance and relevance with min-max scaling
Evaluate a memory system with LoCoMo and LongMemEval and defend it against stale facts and memory injection

lessons.title: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history

blocks.md: From the harness course you know the loop: the model reads a prompt, calls tools, reads the results, and repeats. Everything the model knows during a step is whatever the harness put in the context window. When the session ends, that context is gone. A user who told the assistant last week that they are vegetarian expects it to still know that today.

The naive fix is to paste every past conversation into the prompt. It works for a while, then fails three ways. The history outgrows the context window. Every query pays to re-read the whole history, so cost and latency grow with the relationship. And models use long inputs unevenly: LongMemEval reports that long-context LLMs lose 30% to 60% accuracy when they must answer from a long chat history instead of just the relevant sessions.

**Long-term memory** is the part of an agent that persists across sessions outside the model's weights: a store the harness writes to during or after a conversation and reads from before answering. From the RAG course you already know the read side: embed a query, find similar chunks, put them in the prompt. Memory adds the hard parts RAG mostly skips: deciding *what* to write, *updating* facts that change, and *forgetting*.

blocks.title: Full history in the prompt vs a memory layer (LoCoMo, Mem0 paper)

scenes.caption: Tokens put into the prompt per question. Full context sends the whole conversation, about 26,000 tokens. Mem0 retrieves about 1,764 tokens of memories: over 90% fewer.
Total p95 latency in seconds to answer. Reading 26k tokens every query costs 17.1 s at p95; Mem0 answers in 1.44 s, about 91% lower.
But answer quality (LLM-as-a-Judge score, %) tells a different story: full context still scores highest, 72.90 vs 66.88 for Mem0. Memory buys cost and latency, not free accuracy.

blocks.md: Misconception: a memory layer makes the agent remember *better* than full history. On LoCoMo, where a conversation still fits in the window, full context scored highest in the Mem0 paper. Memory wins when history no longer fits, or when the cost and latency of re-reading it every turn are unacceptable.

What should go into the store? The CoALA framework (Sumers et al.) borrows names from cognitive science. **Working memory** is what is active in the current step, roughly the prompt. **Episodic memory** stores experiences: what happened, when ("on Tuesday the user asked for Lisbon weather"). **Semantic memory** stores knowledge about the world (the user included) and about the agent itself, detached from when it was learned ("the user is vegetarian"). **Procedural memory** is how to act: the model weights and the agent's code and prompts.

blocks.title: Where long-term memory sits in the agent loop

scenes.caption: Without memory, the harness only has this session: the user message goes into the prompt and the LLM answers. Nothing survives the session.
The store keeps two kinds of records. Episodic records are timestamped events; semantic records are distilled facts that stay true until something changes them.
Read path: before calling the LLM, the harness turns the situation into a query, ranks stored memories and puts the best few into the prompt.
Write path: after a turn, new messages are mined for facts worth keeping, checked against what is already stored, and written. Lessons 3 and 4 open up each path.

blocks.md: A memory system is defined by four decisions: what to write, how to reconcile it with what is already stored, what to retrieve for a given step, and what to forget. Retrieval alone is RAG; the write and forget decisions are what make it memory.

blocks.question: A coding assistant learns three things in one session: the user ran the test suite at 14:02 and it failed; the repo uses pnpm, not npm; the user prefers short answers. Which are best stored as semantic memories?
options: All three, because everything the user says is a fact about the user
Only the test failure, because it is the most recent event
The pnpm fact and the short-answer preference; the test run is an episodic event
None; semantic memory only holds facts about the outside world
blocks.explain: The pnpm choice and the answer-length preference stay true until changed, so they are semantic facts. The failing test run at 14:02 is an event tied to a time: episodic. It may matter later ("what failed yesterday?") but it is not a standing fact. CoALA's semantic memory covers knowledge about the agent and the user too, not only the outside world.

blocks.question: A team's support chats average 6,000 tokens and never span sessions. They want lower cost. What is the strongest argument against adding a long-term memory layer?
options: Memory layers cannot run on chats shorter than the context window
Each conversation already fits in context and nothing needs to persist, so memory adds extraction cost and new failure modes for little gain
Vector search is always slower than reading 6,000 tokens
Memory layers always reduce answer accuracy
blocks.explain: Memory pays off when history outgrows the window or must carry across sessions. Here neither holds. Memory is not inherently slower or less accurate; in the Mem0 paper it cut latency sharply while scoring a bit lower than full context. The point is that its benefits do not apply here.

lessons.title: Main context vs external context: paging memory like an OS

blocks.md: MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) frames the problem with an operating-system analogy. An OS gives programs the illusion of more memory than RAM by paging data between RAM and disk. MemGPT gives the LLM the illusion of a bigger context by paging text between **main context** (the prompt tokens, like RAM) and **external context** (databases outside the window, like disk). Anything in external context must be explicitly moved into main context before the model can use it.

Main context has three parts. **System instructions** are read-only and explain the memory hierarchy and the memory functions. **Working context** is a fixed-size read/write block of text for key facts about the user and the agent's persona; only function calls can write it. The **FIFO queue** is a rolling message history, whose first slot holds a recursive summary of messages already evicted. Outside the window sit **recall storage** (every message, ever) and **archival storage** (a read/write database for arbitrary text).

scenes.caption: Main context is the prompt: static instructions, a small editable working context, and the FIFO queue of recent messages. This is all the LLM sees in one inference.
A new message arrives. The queue manager appends it to the FIFO queue and also writes it to recall storage, so no message is ever lost, even after it leaves the window.

Memory pressure: when prompt tokens pass a warning threshold (70% of the window in the paper), the queue manager inserts a system warning. The LLM can now save what matters to working context or archival storage.
Flush: at the flush threshold (100% in the paper) the queue manager evicts a block of messages (for example 50% of the window) and folds them into a new recursive summary at the head of the queue.
Later the user refers to something old. The LLM calls a search function on recall or archival storage; results come back paginated so a single call cannot overflow the window.
Function chaining: a call can set request_heartbeat=true, so the LLM runs again right after the result arrives. That lets it search, read page 2, then answer, all before yielding to the user.

blocks.md: The key idea is **self-editing memory**: the LLM decides what to store, update and search by emitting function calls, and the system executes them and feeds results, including errors such as "working context is full", back into the next step. The paper's own example is a conflicting update. The working context says "Boyfriend named James"; a session later the user writes that they broke up.

blocks.title: Self-editing memory on a changed fact (MemGPT paper, Figure 4)

scenes.caption: An earlier session stored a fact in working context, which sits in every prompt from then on.
Weeks later the user says they broke up. The queue manager logs the message to recall storage automatically.
The agent rewrites the stale fact in place rather than appending a second, contradictory line, then replies consistently.
When the user mentions an old trip, the agent searches recall storage for the original messages instead of relying on its summary.

blocks.md: Current systems keep this split. Letta (formerly MemGPT) keeps core memory in the system prompt every turn (in its current docs, memory files under `system/`) and keeps the rest out of context, where the agent sees a file tree and reads what it needs on demand. Anthropic's memory tool gives Claude a `/memories` directory with `view`, `create`, `str_replace`, `insert`, `delete` and `rename` commands. It is client-side: Claude only requests operations, and your application executes them against storage you control. The docs suggest pairing it with compaction: compaction shrinks the active context, memory keeps what must survive the summary.

blocks.code:
# Anthropic memory tool: Claude requests, your handler executes.
# Tool entry in the request (no schema needed):
tools = [{"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}]

# A tool_use block Claude might emit:
{"command": "str_replace",
 "path": "/memories/user.md",
 "old_str": "Diet: vegetarian",
 "new_str": "Diet: pescatarian (eats fish again)"}

# Your handler must reject any path outside /memories,
# e.g. /memories/../../secrets.env (path traversal).
blocks.caption: The same in-place edit as MemGPT's working_context.replace, expressed as a file edit.

blocks.md: In-context memory (working context, Letta blocks, a memory file the agent always views) is always visible but costs tokens every turn and has a hard size cap. External memory scales without limit but only helps if the agent thinks to search it with the right query. Put small, always-relevant facts in context and everything else outside.

blocks.question: In MemGPT, a message was evicted from the FIFO queue during a flush. Which statement is true?
options: The message is gone; only the recursive summary remains
It is still in the prompt, but compressed
It was moved into working context automatically
It is out of the prompt but still stored in recall storage, reachable through a search function call
blocks.explain: The queue manager writes every message to recall storage when it arrives. Eviction removes it from main context and folds it into the recursive summary, but the original stays in recall storage, which the LLM can search with a function call. Working context only changes when the LLM itself calls a write function.

blocks.question: You give an agent a 2,000-character in-context profile block and an unlimited archival store. Where should "user's company VPN requires the --legacy flag" go if it matters in about one task per month?
options: The in-context block, because in-context facts are always used correctly
Archival storage, because it is rarely needed and would waste always-on block space
Neither; facts that rarely matter should be dropped
Both, so the agent can cross-check them
blocks.explain: The in-context block is paid for on every turn and capped in size, so it should hold small facts that are relevant almost every turn. A monthly detail belongs in external storage, retrieved when a VPN task comes up. Storing it twice creates two copies that can drift apart when one is updated.

lessons.title: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts

blocks.md: MemGPT lets the main agent decide when to write. Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) moves writing into a separate pipeline that runs on every exchange, so the agent does not have to remember to remember. It has two phases: **extraction**, which turns new messages into candidate facts, and **update**, which reconciles each candidate with what is already stored.

Extraction runs on each new message pair (a user message and the assistant reply). An LLM sees a prompt $P = (S, \{m_{t-m}, \dots, m_{t-2}\}, m_{t-1}, m_t)$: a conversation summary $S$ refreshed asynchronously in the background, the last $m$ messages for local context, and the new pair. It returns a short list of salient facts $\Omega = \{\omega_1, \dots, \omega_n\}$. The paper uses $m = 10$.

scenes.caption: Extraction: the new pair plus a global summary and the last 10 messages go to an LLM, which returns candidate facts from the new exchange only.
For each candidate, retrieve the s = 10 most similar existing memories by embedding similarity. Only these neighbors are shown to the next step, not the whole store.
Update: an LLM sees the candidate and its neighbors and picks one operation through a tool call. The store is changed only by these operations.

blocks.md:
The four operations, as the paper defines them:

- **ADD**: no semantically equivalent memory exists, so create a new one.
- **UPDATE**: an existing memory is about the same thing and the candidate adds complementary information, so rewrite it (Mem0's prompt example: "User likes to play cricket" becomes "Loves to play cricket with friends").
- **DELETE**: the candidate contradicts an existing memory, so remove it.
- **NOOP**: the fact is already stored or irrelevant; change nothing. This is deduplication.

Now our running example. The store holds eight memories, M1 to M8 (listed in lesson 4). At hour 200 the user writes: "Heads up, I eat fish again now. And yes, Sam is still allergic to peanuts." Extraction yields two candidates. Each one is compared against its nearest neighbors.

blocks.prompt: The store has M1 "User is vegetarian" and M3 "Sam is allergic to peanuts". Predict the operation chosen for each candidate: "User eats fish" and "Sam is allergic to peanuts".
blocks.reveal: "Sam is allergic to peanuts" is already stored, so it is a **NOOP**; without that check, the store would fill with near-duplicates that crowd out other memories at retrieval time. "User eats fish" contradicts M1, so M1 gets a **DELETE**. In our toy resolver the new fact is then stored as **M9** with an ADD. The paper's DELETE only removes the contradicted memory; whether the new fact is also stored is a prompt design choice, so check what your system does.

blocks.title: The update loop on the hour-200 message
blocks.code:
store = load_store(user_id)          # M1..M8
facts = extract(summary, last_10, new_pair)
for f in facts:
    near = vector_search(store, f, top_s=10)
    op, target = llm_choose_op(f, near)   # tool call
    if op == "ADD":
        store.add(new_id(), f)
    elif op == "UPDATE":
        store.replace(target, f)
    elif op == "DELETE":
        store.remove(target)
        store.add(new_id(), f)      # toy policy: keep new fact
    else:                           # NOOP
        pass

scenes.caption: Extraction returns two candidate facts from the new message. The store still holds M1 to M8.
Candidate 1. Vector search finds M1 "User is vegetarian" among the neighbors. The update LLM judges it a contradiction.
DELETE removes M1. Our toy policy then stores the new fact as M9 so the change itself is remembered.
Candidate 2 matches M3 exactly in meaning. NOOP: nothing is written, so the store does not grow a duplicate.

blocks.md: Deleting is not the only conflict policy, and it destroys history. MemGPT's example overwrote the fact in place ("Ex-boyfriend named James"), which keeps the history in one line. Mem0's graph variant goes further: when a new relationship conflicts with an old one, an LLM resolver marks the old edge **invalid instead of physically removing it**, so the agent can still answer temporal questions like "what did I eat last year?". LongMemEval found that associating timestamps with facts, and using a strong LLM to narrow the search to the right time range, improves recall on temporal-reasoning questions by 6.8% to 11.3%.

Misconception: conflict resolution is a database problem you can solve with "latest write wins". Whether two facts conflict is a judgment about meaning ("eats fish" vs "vegetarian" share no words), which is why Mem0 asks an LLM. That also means the resolver can be wrong: a sarcastic "oh sure, I love meetings" can delete a real preference.

blocks.question: The store holds "User likes hiking". A new message yields the candidate "User goes hiking in the Alps every summer with their brother". Which operation fits Mem0's definitions?
options: ADD, because the sentence is new
DELETE, because the old memory is less precise
UPDATE, because it is the same topic with complementary detail
NOOP, because the user already likes hiking
blocks.explain: UPDATE is for augmenting an existing memory with complementary information, like the paper's cricket example. ADD would leave two overlapping memories (a deduplication failure). DELETE is for contradictions, and nothing here contradicts. NOOP would lose the new details.

blocks.question: Why does Mem0 retrieve the top s similar memories before choosing an operation, instead of showing the update LLM the whole store?
options: Because the LLM can only output one operation per call
Because the store can be far larger than a prompt, and duplicates or contradictions are almost always about the same topic, so similarity search finds them cheaply
Because similar memories are always duplicates and can be deleted
Because embedding search decides the operation, and the LLM only formats it
blocks.explain: The store grows without bound, so the update step needs a small candidate set. Conflicts and duplicates are about the same subject, which embedding similarity surfaces. The LLM, not the search, decides the operation; similar does not mean duplicate.

lessons.title: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance

blocks.md: RAG ranks chunks by similarity to the query. An agent's memory needs more. A memory from five minutes ago is more likely to matter than one from last year, and "Sam is allergic to peanuts" should outrank "user had pasta for lunch" even when both are somewhat related. Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) keeps a **memory stream**: a list of records, each with a natural language description, a creation timestamp and a most recent access timestamp. Retrieval scores every record on three signals.

- **Recency**: exponential decay over the hours since the memory was last retrieved, with decay factor 0.995 per hour.
- **Importance**: an integer from 1 (mundane, like brushing teeth) to 10 (poignant, like a breakup), rated by the LLM once, when the memory is created. The paper reports 2 for "cleaning up the room" and 8 for "asking your crush out on a date".
- **Relevance**: cosine similarity between the memory's embedding and the query's embedding.

blocks.caption: Each signal is min-max scaled to [0, 1] across the candidate memories, then summed. The paper sets all alphas to 1 and puts the top-ranked memories that fit the context window into the prompt.

scenes.caption: At 0.995 per hour, recency keeps 0.887 after a day and 0.431 after a week. Its half-life is ln 0.5 / ln 0.995, about 138 hours.
A faster decay, 0.98 per hour, has a half-life of about 34 hours: the agent's attention snaps to the last day or so.
A slow decay, 0.999 per hour, has a half-life of about 693 hours (four weeks). Recency barely separates memories, so importance and relevance dominate.

blocks.md:
Our toy store at hour 200. The query is "book dinner for me and Sam on Friday". To keep it small, assume no memory has been retrieved since it was created, so last access equals creation time. The cosine values are given, as an embedding model would return them.

1. M1 "User is vegetarian": 198 h ago, importance 8, cosine 0.62
2. M2 "Had pasta for lunch": 50 h, 2, 0.41
3. M3 "Sam is allergic to peanuts": 140 h, 9, 0.55
4. M4 "Asked about Lisbon weather": 10 h, 2, 0.08
5. M5 "Favorite restaurant is Nopa": 80 h, 6, 0.71
6. M6 "Busy Friday until 7pm": 2 h, 5, 0.66
7. M7 "Moved to Oakland": 170 h, 7, 0.35
8. M8 "Complained about slow wifi": 25 h, 3, 0.05

blocks.title: The three signals after min-max scaling

scenes.caption: Raw recency runs from 0.371 (M1, 198 h) to 0.990 (M6, 2 h). Min-max scaling maps the oldest to 0 and the newest to 1, everything else in between.
Importance runs from 2 to 9, so M2 and M4 (both 2) scale to 0 and M3 (9) to 1. M1 at 8 becomes (8 - 2) / 7 = 0.86.
Relevance runs from cosine 0.05 (wifi) to 0.71 (Nopa). Note how M4 and M8 are very recent but irrelevant: recency alone would put them near the top.
M6 is strong on all three; M1 has zero recency but high importance and relevance. The sum decides.

blocks.prompt: With all weights equal to 1, which memory ranks first, and does M4 (Lisbon weather, 10 hours old) make the top 5?
blocks.reveal: M6 "Busy Friday until 7pm" wins with 1.00 + 0.43 + 0.92 = 2.35. The top 5 are M6 2.35, M5 2.05, M3 1.96, M1 1.72, M7 1.26. M4 scores only 0.98: its high recency (0.94) cannot make up for zero importance and near-zero relevance. Ranking by recency alone would have put M4 second.

blocks.title: Building up the retrieval score (top 5 go into the prompt)

scenes.caption: Recency only: the newest memories (M6, M4, M8) dominate, and two of them are useless for booking dinner.
Add importance: M3 (peanut allergy, 9) and M1 (vegetarian, 8) climb, while mundane recent events stay low.
Add relevance for the full score. Top 5: M6, M5, M3, M1, M7. Totals are computed from unrounded parts, so a few differ from the rounded sum by 0.01.

blocks.md: Now apply the write from lesson 3. Suppose the store had skipped conflict resolution and simply appended M9 "User eats fish now" (created at hour 200, importance 8, cosine 0.64) next to M1. M9 is the newest and very relevant, so it scores 2.75 and ranks first. But M1 still scores 1.72 and also makes the top 5. The prompt now says both "vegetarian" and "eats fish".

blocks.title: A conflicting fact, unresolved vs resolved

scenes.caption: Both kept: top 5 are M9 2.75, M6 2.34, M5 2.05, M3 1.96 and M1 1.72. The model sees two contradictory diet facts and must guess which is current.
Resolved (M1 deleted, M9 added): top 5 are M9, M6, M5, M3 and M7. Removing M1 also changes the min-max range, so M3's scaled recency drops from 0.20 to 0.12 although M3 itself did not change.

blocks.md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

blocks.question: Generative Agents measures recency from a memory's last *access*, not its creation. After this query retrieves M6, M5, M3, M1 and M7, what happens on the next query an hour later?
options: Nothing changes; recency only depends on creation time
The retrieved memories get recency 0.995 raw, so they gain an edge: frequently retrieved memories tend to stay retrievable
The retrieved memories are demoted so the agent sees different ones next time
Importance is re-rated for the retrieved memories
blocks.explain: Retrieval updates the last-access timestamp, so one hour later those five have raw recency 0.995 while the rest keep decaying. This is a rich-get-richer effect: it keeps active topics in view, but it can also lock in an early mistake. Importance is rated once, at creation.

blocks.question: A teammate sets the recency weight to 3 and the others to 1 to make the agent "feel more present". For the dinner query, which memory is most at risk of being pushed out of the top 5?
options: M6, busy Friday
M4, Lisbon weather
M1, vegetarian (198 hours old)
M8, slow wifi
blocks.explain: M1's scaled recency is 0, so tripling recency adds nothing to it (still 1.72), while every recent memory gains twice its recency: M4 rises to about 2.86, M8 to 2.62 and M2 to 2.52. The new top 5 is M6, M5, M4, M8, M2, so the dietary fact drops out (M3, the peanut allergy, falls to sixth too). Recent trivia gains; old, important facts lose.

lessons.title: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion

blocks.md: Raw observations are a poor basis for judgment. The Generative Agents paper's example: asked whom Klaus would most like to spend an hour with, an agent with only observations picks Wolfgang, the dorm neighbor Klaus meets most often, because frequent mentions dominate retrieval. What it needs is a higher-level conclusion, such as "Klaus is passionate about research", which no single observation states. **Reflection** writes such conclusions back into memory.

The mechanism has precise rules. Reflection triggers when the sum of importance scores of the latest perceived events exceeds a threshold (150 in their implementation); agents reflected roughly two or three times a simulated day. The agent takes the 100 most recent records and asks the LLM for the 3 most salient high-level questions. Each question becomes a retrieval query. The LLM then writes insights that cite their evidence, like "Klaus Mueller is dedicated to his research on gentrification (because of 1, 2, 8, 15)".

blocks.title: A reflection tree: observations at the leaves, insights above

nodes.label:
Q: What is Klaus
passionate about?

scenes.caption: The memory stream holds observations. Each is narrow; none says what Klaus cares about.
Importance has accumulated past the threshold. From the 100 most recent records the LLM proposes questions, such as what Klaus is passionate about.
The question retrieves evidence; the LLM writes an insight that keeps pointers to the cited records. The insight is stored in the same stream and competes in retrieval like any memory.
Reflections can cite other reflections, so the stream grows into a tree whose upper nodes are more abstract. Ablations in the paper rated agents without reflection as less believable.

blocks.md: In our toy store the importance scores sum to 42, and 50 after M9. With a threshold of 150 no reflection fires yet. Production systems run the same idea as background work. Mem0 refreshes its conversation summary asynchronously so extraction does not wait. Letta calls it **dreaming**: background subagents review recent conversations, consolidate lessons and update memory, triggered after a number of steps or on context compaction.

Consolidation adds memories; **forgetting** removes or demotes them. MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2023) uses an Ebbinghaus-style curve: retention $R = e^{-t/S}$, where $t$ is time since the memory was learned or last recalled and $S$ is its strength. $S$ starts at 1; each recall adds 1 to $S$ and resets $t$ to 0, so memories that keep being used fade more slowly. The authors call it an exploratory, highly simplified model.

blocks.title: MemoryBank retention: recalls make memories fade slower

scenes.caption: A memory mentioned once (S = 1) keeps 0.368 after t = 1 and 0.135 after t = 2. Without recalls it is soon a forgetting candidate.
Recalled twice more (S = 3), it keeps 0.717 at t = 1 and 0.368 at t = 3. Every recall also resets t to 0.
Simplified model: real systems also forget by explicit rules, such as expiring files nobody has opened for a long time, which Anthropic's memory tool docs suggest.

blocks.md: Some forgetting is not optional. When a user asks to be forgotten, "lower its score" is not enough. Mem0's delete API, for instance, removes single memories, batches, or everything matching a user filter, and its docs frame this as how you honor erasure requests such as GDPR and CCPA. The catch is **derived memory**. A reflection cites the observations it came from, a MemGPT recursive summary absorbs evicted messages, and an UPDATE merges old text into new. Deleting the source record leaves its content alive in those derivatives.

Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

blocks.question: A user's running sum of importance since the last reflection is 50. Each new event in a quiet week is rated 2. Using the paper's threshold, roughly how many such events until the next reflection fires?
options: About 50 events, since the sum must exceed 150
About 3 events, since reflection fires two or three times a day
Never, because low-importance events are not counted
About 75 events, since the threshold is 150 and each event adds 2
blocks.explain: The sum must climb from 50 to over 150, so it needs more than 100 more points: 51 events at 2 each take it to 152. Two or three reflections a day was what the paper observed in its busy simulated town, not a fixed schedule. 75 events ignores the 50 already accumulated. Every event's importance is summed.

blocks.question: A user asks the agent to forget that they were treated for a medical condition. The raw observation is deleted. Which leftover is the most likely leak?
options: The embedding model's weights
A reflection such as "User has been managing a chronic illness" that cited the deleted observation
The system prompt
The recency score of the deleted memory
blocks.explain: Reflections, summaries and merged facts are new records that contain the content of their sources. Unless deletion follows their source pointers, they survive and get retrieved. Embedding model weights were not trained on the user's data, and a deleted memory's score disappears with it.

lessons.title: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails

blocks.md: How do you know a memory system works? Ordinary QA benchmarks fit in one context. Memory benchmarks build long, multi-session histories and ask questions whose answers are buried in them. **LoCoMo** (Maharana et al., 2024) has very long-term conversations of about 300 turns and 9K tokens on average, over up to 35 sessions. (The Mem0 paper, whose numbers lesson 1 showed, reports about 26,000 tokens per conversation on its LoCoMo setup.) It tests question answering in five categories (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, commonsense or world knowledge, adversarial), event summarization and multimodal dialogue generation.

**LongMemEval** (Wu et al., ICLR 2025) targets chat assistants with 500 hand-made questions over five abilities: **information extraction**, **multi-session reasoning**, **temporal reasoning**, **knowledge updates** (noticing that the user's information changed) and **abstention** (answering "I don't know" when the fact was never mentioned). Histories are scalable: LongMemEval_S has about 115k tokens per question, LongMemEval_M has 500 sessions, about 1.5M tokens.

LongMemEval also frames any memory system as three stages: **indexing** (what to store and under what keys), **retrieval**, and **reading** (using what was retrieved). Its findings map onto this course. Storing history per conversation round beat storing whole sessions. Compressing everything into extracted user facts lost information overall, though it helped multi-session reasoning. Expanding index keys with extracted facts raised recall@k by 9.4%. Even with perfect recall, reading strategy (such as Chain-of-Note and structured formats) moved QA accuracy by up to 10 points.

scenes.caption: Baselines answer a question about sessions 1 to 5 of a chat from a lossy summary of those sessions. Accuracy is 32% to 39%.
MemGPT searches the full history through paginated recall queries and reaches 92.5% with GPT-4. The underlying model matters: with GPT-3.5 Turbo, MemGPT reaches 66.9%.

blocks.md: Read memory benchmark numbers with care. Many are judged by an LLM, baselines differ (a lossy summary vs full context), and LoCoMo conversations fit in modern context windows. Evaluate on your own traffic too: plant facts, change some later, ask about some never stated, and score knowledge updates and abstention separately from plain recall.

The common failure modes follow from the mechanics:

- **Stale facts**: a preference changed but the old memory still scores high (lesson 4).
- **Contradictions**: both versions are retrieved and the model picks one, sometimes the wrong one.
- **Bad writes**: extraction stores a joke, a hypothetical ("if I were vegan...") or the assistant's own guess as a user fact; it then persists across sessions.
- **Over-retrieval**: irrelevant memories in the prompt distract the model or leak personal details into unrelated answers.
- **Bloat**: no NOOP or forgetting, so near-duplicates crowd out useful memories.

The most dangerous one is **prompt injection via stored memory**. Greshake et al. (2023) showed indirect injection, where instructions hidden in content the model reads (a web page, an email) take over the model. With memory, an injection can **persist**: in their demonstration, a compromised agent stored the injection in a key-value memory; after the agent was reset, a user asked it to read the last conversation from memory, and it re-poisoned itself in the new session. The user who triggers it may not be the one who planted it.

blocks.title: Persistence attack: one poisoned page, every future session

scenes.caption: Session 1: the user asks for a summary of a page. The page hides text addressed to the model.
The write path treats the injected text as a user preference and stores it. Nothing marks where the memory came from.
Session 2, days later, a fresh context. Retrieval loads the poisoned memory into the prompt as if it were trusted user knowledge.

blocks.md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

Anthropic's memory tool docs list the operational side of the same discipline: validate every path so a request like `/memories/../../secrets.env` cannot escape the memory directory, strip sensitive data before writing, cap file sizes and how much a `view` returns, and periodically delete memory files that have not been accessed in a long time.

blocks.question: Your memory system scores well on recall but often answers with an old address after users move. Which LongMemEval ability is failing, and where would you fix it first?
options: Abstention; add a confidence threshold to the reader
Information extraction; use a bigger embedding model
Knowledge updates; fix the write path so a new address updates or invalidates the old one, and keep timestamps
Multi-session reasoning; retrieve more memories per query
blocks.explain: Recognizing that the user's information changed is LongMemEval's knowledge-update ability. Recall is fine, so a better retriever or more results would only surface both addresses. The fix is on the write path (UPDATE, DELETE or invalidation) plus timestamps so the reader can tell which is current.

blocks.question: Which defense addresses the persistence attack most directly?
options: Store a source tag on every memory and never treat tool- or web-derived memories as user instructions
Use a larger context window so the memory store is not needed
Lower the recency decay so old memories fade faster
Run reflection more often so injected memories get summarized away
blocks.explain: The attack works because text from an untrusted web page is written and later read back as trusted user knowledge. Provenance breaks that chain. Faster decay only delays it (and retrieval refreshes recency), reflection can copy the injection into new derived memories, and a larger window does not remove the cross-session store the attack lives in.
